questions.prompt: How does Martin Fowler define software architecture?

options.text: Those decisions which are both important and hard to change
The set of all classes in a project
The user interface layout
The CI/CD pipeline configuration

questions.explanation: Fowler: software architecture is those decisions which are both important and hard to change — it is a communication tool for shared understanding.

questions.prompt: The CAP theorem states a distributed data system can simultaneously provide at most how many of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance?

options.text: Two of the three
All three
Only one
None under partition

questions.explanation: CAP (Brewer's) theorem: a distributed data system can simultaneously provide at most two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.

questions.prompt: How do scalability and elasticity differ in cloud computing?

options.text: Scalability adds resources on a planned/permanent basis; elasticity dynamically scales up/down in real time to match demand
They are exactly the same thing
Elasticity is always permanent; scalability is temporary
Scalability only applies to storage

questions.explanation: Scalability handles increased workload by adding resources on a planned/permanent basis; elasticity is automated real-time scaling up/down to match fluctuating demand.

questions.prompt: A main goal of CI/CD is to keep the main branch 'green' at all times, promoting small iterative changes and avoiding big merges.
questions.explanation: CI/CD keeps the main branch green, integrating code often and deploying frequently with small, easy-to-rollback changes; most validations should happen before the merge.

questions.prompt: Which type of quality does the customer NOT directly see or buy, corresponding to technical debt?

options.text: Internal quality
External quality
Functional requirements
User experience

questions.explanation: Internal quality is what the customer doesn't buy or see; neglecting it accumulates technical debt, while external quality is customer-facing.

questions.prompt: Which techniques are recommended to scale the request path?

options.text: Cache hot reads to reduce repeated read pressure
Use asynchronous messaging / queue-based load leveling for slow or bursty work
Throttle to preserve SLOs under load
Remove all monitoring

questions.explanation: Scale the request path by caching hot reads, queuing slow work, and throttling to protect the critical path; caching does not replace throttling.

questions.prompt: What is 'the first rule of sharding'?

options.text: Don't shard until you absolutely have to
Always shard from day one
Shard only the cache
Never use indexing before sharding

questions.explanation: The first rule of sharding is: don't shard until you absolutely have to; prefer tuning, indexing, partitioning, and polyglot persistence first.

questions.prompt: Which are common drivers that can trigger architectural change?

options.text: Business model expansion (market/geography)
Delivery friction
Reliability pain and data/compliance pressure
Having too few lines of code

questions.explanation: Common drivers: business model expansion, delivery friction, reliability pain, data/compliance pressure, and organization scaling.

questions.prompt: A key takeaway is to document architecture decisions using ADRs and prefer iterative, incremental changes over big-bang changes.
questions.explanation: Takeaways: document with ADRs, prefer iterative/incremental changes (no big bang), let data drive decisions, run workshops, and measure success before/after.

questions.prompt: How do vertical and horizontal compute scaling differ?

options.text: Vertical scaling adds memory/CPU to a machine (scaling up); horizontal adds more nodes (scaling out)
Vertical scaling adds more nodes; horizontal adds memory/CPU
They both only apply to storage
They are the same thing

questions.explanation: VMs scale vertically by adding memory/CPU (scaling up); adding more nodes is horizontal scaling (scaling out), also enabled by containers and functions.

questions.prompt: What is a Service-Level Agreement (SLA)?

options.text: A legal contract defining what a customer should expect from the provider, e.g. availability (number of 9s)
A profiling tool built into the JVM
A type of database index
An event payload format

questions.explanation: An SLA is a legal document/contract defining what a customer should expect from a SaaS provider, such as the amount of available time (number of 9s).

questions.prompt: Static code analysis in the CI/CD pipeline is used to PREVENT bad code from reaching the main branch via quality gates.
questions.explanation: Running static code analysis with quality gates inside CI/CD prevents bad code from reaching the master/main branch — the same idea applies to agentic coding.

questions.prompt: How is high availability typically achieved in the cloud per the deck?

options.text: Deploying across multiple Availability Zones (and regions) for redundancy and disaster recovery
Running a single large server
Disabling replication
Sharding from day one

questions.explanation: High availability and disaster recovery use multiple Availability Zones (Multi-AZ) and regions; CAP reminds us a distributed system trades among consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.

questions.prompt: How does the cost of finding/fixing bugs change across the SDLC stages?

options.text: It increases the later it is found (idea → requirement → development → testing → production)
It is constant at every stage
It decreases towards production
It only matters at the idea stage

questions.explanation: The cost of finding bugs rises across stages from idea through requirements, development, integration, and testing, peaking in production.

questions.prompt: Which items are part of Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)?

options.text: Infrastructure and development team costs
Licenses and development tools costs
Training, support, and maintenance
The number of git branches

questions.explanation: TCO includes infrastructure, development team, licenses, tools, training, support, marketing/sales, fixed costs, taxes, maintenance, and security.

questions.prompt: Which architectural traits support the SaaS upsell/cross-sell business model?

options.text: Modular architecture, feature composition, feature toggling, and regional customizations
A single hard-coded feature set for all customers
One-off on-prem licenses only
Disabling all configuration

questions.explanation: The SaaS model (MRR, freemium) leans on modular architecture, feature composition, feature toggling, dynamic feature sets, and regional customizations to enable upsell/cross-sell.

questions.prompt: How does the deck summarise Conway's Law in practice?

options.text: The structure of the design reflects how people communicate and are organised
Software always expands to fill available memory
More developers always means faster delivery
Every system eventually becomes a monolith

questions.explanation: Conway's Law: organisations are constrained to produce designs that copy their communication structures — the design reflects how teams communicate and work together.

questions.prompt: According to the test automation pyramid, how do unit tests compare with UI tests?

options.text: Unit tests are stable, quick to run, and easy to build; UI tests are less stable, time-consuming, and resource-intensive
UI tests are the cheapest and most stable
Unit tests are the slowest layer
Both layers cost the same

questions.explanation: In the test automation pyramid, unit tests are stable, quick, and easy to build, while UI tests are less stable, time-consuming, resource-intensive, and harder to build.

questions.prompt: In the persona example, which description fits 'Tom'?

options.text: Seasonal usage, heavy on data reads, performance-focused, unstructured queries, few users
Continuous usage, data-driven and structured, integration/process focused
Less frequent access, heavy on data input/writes, UX-focused
No data access at all

questions.explanation: Tom: seasonal usage, heavy on data reads, performance-focused, unstructured queries, few users; Jim is write/UX-heavy and Sarah is continuous, data-driven, integration-focused.

questions.prompt: How does Microsoft's guidance describe throttling relative to caching?

options.text: Throttling is a self-preservation control loop, and caching does not replace throttling
Caching fully replaces the need for throttling
Throttling and caching are the same mechanism
Throttling should be avoided under load

questions.explanation: Throttling is explicitly a self-preservation control loop to preserve SLOs under load; caching reduces read pressure but does not replace throttling.

questions.prompt: Where do the DORA metrics referenced in the deck originate?

options.text: The 2019 Accelerate State of DevOps report (Google Cloud / Nicole Forsgren)
The C4 model documentation
ISO/IEC 15939
The Gang of Four book

questions.explanation: The DORA metrics are cited from the 2019 Accelerate State of DevOps report (Google Cloud, Nicole Forsgren) on elite performance, productivity, and scaling.
